title: Neutrinos From Inside the Earth Are Mapping the Mantle
hook: You can't drill to the mantle, but its radioactive decays leak neutrinos straight through the planet — and detectors are starting to read them.
key_points: Radioactive uranium and thorium inside Earth emit antineutrinos as they decay; these "geoneutrinos" pass through rock almost unimpeded.
Their number and energy spectrum reveal how much radioactive material the planet holds and roughly where it sits.
That matters because radioactive decay supplies a large share of the internal heat that drives mantle convection and plate tectonics.
A worldwide network of neutrino detectors is now pooling data to build a picture no seismic survey or borehole can provide.
The technique turns particle detectors built for physics into instruments for geology.
content_html: Nobody has ever sampled Earth's mantle directly; the deepest boreholes barely dent the crust. But the mantle is radioactive, and radioactive decay emits neutrinos, and neutrinos ignore rock. A global constellation of neutrino detectors is now assembling a view of the radioactive elements powering the planet's heat engine.
extra_html: Uranium and thorium deep inside Earth decay continuously, releasing antineutrinos known as geoneutrinos. Because these particles interact so feebly, essentially all of them stream out of the planet unimpeded — carrying, in their number and energy spectrum, a census of how much radioactive material lies below and roughly how it is distributed. That census is a live geological question. Radioactive decay contributes a large share of Earth's internal heat, and that heat drives mantle convection, which in turn drives plate tectonics, volcanism, and mountain-building. Estimates of the total have long relied on indirect arguments from meteorite composition and heat-flow measurements. Detectors built to study neutrino physics can now weigh in directly, though the signal is so faint that no single site suffices; the picture emerges only from combining detectors around the world, each seeing a different blend of nearby crust and distant mantle. As Quanta's James Dinneen reports, it amounts to geology done with particle physics instruments.

related.title: Radioactivity and Half-Life
related.hook: You can't predict when a single unstable atom will decay, yet a huge sample decays on a clock so precise we use it to date rocks billions of years old.

related.title: Catching the Ghost Particle
related.hook: Trillions of neutrinos stream through your body every second, yet they almost never touch anything. To catch even a few, physicists build some of the most audacious detectors ever conceived.

related.title: JUNO's First Look at Shape-Shifting Neutrinos
related.hook: A giant detector buried under China caught neutrinos changing identity mid-flight — and in just 59 days made one of the sharpest measurements yet of the ghost particle's habits.

flashcards.prompt: What is a geoneutrino, and why can it tell us about the deep Earth?
flashcards.back_html: An antineutrino emitted by radioactive decay of uranium and thorium inside the planet. Neutrinos pass through rock almost unimpeded, so they carry information out from depths nothing else reaches.

flashcards.prompt: Why does counting Earth's radioactive material matter for geology?

choices.text: Radioactive decay supplies much of the internal heat that drives mantle convection and plate tectonics
It sets the strength of Earth's magnetic field directly
It determines the length of Earth's day

flashcards.explanation_html: The planet's heat engine is what moves plates and builds mountains, and radioactive decay is a major part of its fuel budget — so the amount and distribution of uranium and thorium is a first-order geological question.

flashcards.prompt: Why does studying geoneutrinos require a global network rather than one detector?
flashcards.back_html: Geoneutrino signals are extremely faint, and each detector sees a different mix of local crust and deep mantle — so combining sites worldwide is what makes a planet-wide picture possible.
